units.t: Confirmation Bias.
Part one. The two, four, six puzzle.
Let's start with a puzzle you can play along with right now.
I'm thinking of a rule that some sequences of three numbers follow.
Here's one sequence that fits my rule.
Two, four, six.
Your job is to work out the rule.
You can test it by suggesting other sequences of three numbers, and I'll tell you whether each one fits.
What would you try first?
Most people suggest something like eight, ten, twelve.
Yes, that fits.
Then maybe twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four.
Yes, that fits too.
Then one hundred, one hundred and two, one hundred and four.
Fits again. At this point, most people feel confident.
The rule must be numbers going up by two.
But that isn't the rule.
The rule is simply any three numbers in ascending order.
One, two, three fits.
So does five, nineteen, four hundred.
Numbers going up by two was only ever one small example of the real rule.
This puzzle was created by a British psychologist called Peter Wason, and he published his results in 1960.
What fascinated him wasn't that people guessed wrong.
It was how they went about testing their guesses.
Nearly everyone tested sequences that they expected to fit their idea.
Almost nobody tried a sequence that might break it, like three, two, one, or one, two, ninety-nine.
In Wason's study, only a minority of people found the correct rule on their first announced guess.
Here's the key point.
If you only ever look for evidence that you're right, you can collect a mountain of it and still be wrong.
Every yes felt like progress.
But none of those yeses could ever show that the idea was mistaken.
The most useful test would have been one designed to prove the idea wrong.
This tendency has a name.
Confirmation bias. It's the habit of searching for, noticing, interpreting and remembering information in ways that support what we already believe.
It's one of the most studied thinking errors in all of psychology, and it isn't a sign of low intelligence.
Clever people do it too.
Sometimes clever people are even better at it, because they're better at building arguments for what they already think.
The idea itself is old.
Around four hundred years ago, the English philosopher Francis Bacon described it beautifully.
In his book the Novum Organum, published in 1620, he wrote that the human understanding, once it has adopted an opinion, draws all things else to support and agree with it.
In other words, our minds don't just hold beliefs.
They recruit evidence for them.
Why would our minds work this way?
One reasonable explanation is efficiency.
Checking every belief from scratch would be exhausting.
Most of the time, our existing beliefs are good enough, so it makes sense to lean on them.
Looking for a quick yes is fast and usually harmless.
The trouble starts when the belief is wrong, or when the stakes are high, and our shortcut quietly keeps us from finding out.
There's an emotional side too.
Being right feels good.
Being wrong can sting, especially when a belief is tied up with who we are, our politics, our job, our choices as a parent.
Evidence that we're wrong can feel less like information and more like an attack.
So we steer around it, often without noticing.
In the next part, we'll look at the three main ways confirmation bias works on us.
It isn't just about what we search for.
It also changes how we read evidence, and even what we remember.
Part two. Search, interpret, remember.
Confirmation bias shows up in three places.
How we search for information.
How we interpret it.
And how we remember it.
Let's take them one at a time.
First, search. The two, four, six puzzle was all about search.
We ask questions that we expect to answer yes.
You see this everywhere in daily life.
If you suspect a new colleague is lazy, you'll notice every late arrival and long lunch.
You won't go looking for the evening they stayed back to fix a problem.
If you've decided a certain car brand is unreliable, you'll search online for breakdown stories, and of course, you'll find plenty.
The internet makes this easier than ever.
Almost any belief can find a website that agrees with it.
Second, interpretation. This one is sneakier.
Even when two people look at exactly the same evidence, they can walk away more convinced of opposite conclusions.
A famous study at Stanford University in 1979 showed this clearly.
The researchers, Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper, gathered people who either strongly supported or strongly opposed the death penalty.
They gave everyone the same two studies to read.
One study seemed to show that the death penalty deters crime.
The other seemed to show it doesn't.
It was a balanced set of evidence.
You might expect people to move towards the middle.
The opposite happened.
Supporters rated the pro study as more convincing and picked holes in the other.
Opponents did exactly the reverse.
And after reading the same mixed evidence, both groups reported feeling more strongly about their original view.
Same facts, opposite conclusions, and more confidence all round.
Why? Because we don't treat evidence evenly.
When something agrees with us, we ask, can I believe this?
And usually the answer is yes.
When something disagrees with us, we ask a much tougher question.
Must I believe this?
And it's almost always possible to find a reason why not.
Third, memory. Our memories don't store events evenly either.
In a study by Mark Snyder and Nancy Cantor, people read a story about a woman called Jane, who did some things that seemed outgoing and some things that seemed shy.
Days later, some people were asked whether Jane would suit a job as a real estate agent.
Others were asked whether she'd suit a job as a librarian.
Each group mostly remembered the parts of the story that fitted the question they were asked.
The real estate group recalled her outgoing moments.
The librarian group recalled her quiet ones.
Same Jane, different memories.
This is why horoscopes and psychic readings can feel so accurate.
We remember the hits and quietly forget the misses.
The prediction that came true feels meaningful.
The ten that didn't simply fade away.
There's a modern twist on all of this.
Many of the apps and feeds we use are designed to show us more of what we already click on.
If you watch a few videos with one view on a topic, you'll probably be offered more that agree.
Nobody has to be trying to mislead you.
The feed is simply giving you more of what you seem to like.
But the effect can be a bit like playing the two, four, six game with a partner who only ever hands you sequences that fit your guess.
Put these three together and you get a powerful loop.
We search for evidence that fits.
We interpret mixed evidence in our favour.
And we remember the bits that agreed with us.
Each step makes the belief feel stronger, even when the world hasn't given us any new reason to hold it.
So can we do anything about it?
The good news is yes.
In the final part, we'll look at some simple habits that researchers have found genuinely help.
Part three. How to catch yourself.
The first thing to know is that simply telling yourself to be fair doesn't work very well.
In a follow-up study, Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston tried exactly that.
They asked some people to be as objective and unbiased as possible when weighing evidence.
It made little difference.
People sincerely believed they were being fair, and they were still biased.
What did work was a more specific instruction.
The researchers asked another group to consider the opposite.
In effect, they said, as you read each study, ask yourself how you'd judge it if it had found the opposite result.
That simple question cut the bias noticeably.
It forced people to apply the same standards to both sides.
So here's the first habit.
Consider the opposite.
When you find yourself nodding along to something, ask, if this said the reverse, would I accept it this easily?
And when you find yourself picking holes in something, ask, would I be this picky if I agreed with it?
The second habit is to go looking for disconfirming evidence on purpose.
This is exactly what the two, four, six puzzle rewarded.
Instead of asking, what would prove me right, ask, what would prove me wrong, and where could I find it?
If you think a business idea is brilliant, don't just ask friends who'll say it's great.
Ask someone likely to spot the flaws.
If you're convinced about a health claim, look for the best argument against it, not the worst one.
Charles Darwin had a lovely version of this.
In his autobiography, he described what he called a golden rule.
Whenever he came across a published fact or a new thought that went against his general results, he wrote a note about it straight away.
He'd learned from experience that facts like that were far more likely to slip from his memory than the ones that supported him.
Darwin was deliberately working against his own memory bias.
The third habit is to hold beliefs with a little looseness.
Try putting a rough confidence level on the things you believe.
Instead of, I'm right about this, try, I'm about seventy per cent sure.
It sounds like a small change.
But it leaves room for new evidence to move you, and it makes changing your mind feel like an update rather than a defeat.
It's worth knowing that this matters well beyond arguments over dinner.
In medicine, doctors are trained to watch for something called premature closure.
That's when a diagnosis is settled on early, and later symptoms get explained to fit it rather than questioned.
In investing, people who've bought a share often read good news about it closely and skim past the warning signs.
In workplaces, a first impression of a new employee can shape how every later piece of their work is judged.
In each case, the fix is the same.
Build a moment into the process where someone deliberately asks, what else could explain this?
And finally, be a bit gentle with other people.
Once you understand confirmation bias, it's tempting to spot it in everyone else.
That's actually confirmation bias about confirmation bias.
Everyone has it, including you and me.
The goal isn't to win arguments.
It's to be a little less wrong over time.
Let's recap the three big takeaways.
First, confirmation bias affects how we search for evidence, how we interpret it, and what we remember.
Second, just trying to be fair isn't enough, but asking yourself to consider the opposite really helps.
Third, the most useful evidence is the kind that could prove you wrong, so go looking for it on purpose, the way Darwin did.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In Peter Wason's puzzle, the example sequence was two, four, six. What was the actual rule?
Answer. Any three numbers in ascending order.
Question two. In the Stanford death penalty study, what happened after both sides read the same mixed evidence?
Answer. Both sides became more convinced of their original views.
Question three. What simple instruction reduced bias better than being told to be objective?
Answer. Consider the opposite. Ask how you'd judge the evidence if it had found the reverse result.
That's the end of Confirmation Bias. Nicely done.
